title: How to Clean and Oil Skate Bearings So They Stay Fast
thumbnail_text: Your bearings are slow because of this

scenes.heading: How to Clean and Oil Skate Bearings
scenes.sub: A twenty minute routine that keeps them fast
scenes.narration: By the end of this, you will know how to clean and oil your skate bearings properly, in about twenty minutes. You will also know which solvents are safe, which ones quietly ruin a bearing, and when to stop cleaning and replace them. Bearing care is easy and costs almost nothing. It is also the highest return piece of skate care there is. Yet most skaters never do it, or do it badly enough that they would have been better off leaving their bearings alone. The principles are the same for steel or ceramic, inline or quad, so this routine keeps whatever you own rolling like day one.

scenes.heading: Where speed is lost
scenes.narration: A bearing is a simple machine. Balls run between two raceways. A cage holds them in place, and seals protect the whole thing. Look at the two raceways on screen. When the raceway is clean and lightly oiled, the ball rolls. When a hard particle gets onto that raceway, the ball starts to skid and grind instead. Every one of those tiny skids is speed you paid for and did not get. Worse, a particle scores the surface, and that score collects more dirt. So a dirty bearing does not just stay slow. It keeps getting slower.

scenes.heading: Three things slow your bearings
bullets: Dust, grit and road film
Water that flushes out the oil
Old or wrong lubricant
scenes.narration: Three things cause the decline, and they make each other worse. First, contamination. Dust, grit and road film work their way past the seals over time. Second, water. Water is worse than dirt. It flushes the lubricant out and leaves bare steel, and steel plus water plus time means rust. One skate through a puddle can undo a season of care if you do not deal with it that evening. Third, old or wrong lubricant. Oil breaks down and turns into a paste that slows you more than the dirt does. And a heavy garage oil in a speed bearing is like running in wet sand.

scenes.heading: Steps one to three: remove, open, clean
bullets: Push bearings out, never hammer
Ease seals out from the inner edge
Wash in one jar, rinse in another
Spin by hand, never with air
scenes.narration: Set aside twenty minutes and work in good light. Step one. Take the wheels off and push the bearings out with a bearing puller or the end of an axle. Never lever against the inner race with anything sharp, and never hammer. Keep them in order, because if one position keeps wearing out bearings, that usually points to a frame or axle problem. Step two. If your seals come out, ease them out from the inner edge with a fine pin. Go gently, because a bent seal never sits right again. Step three. Agitate the bearings in solvent in a sealed jar, then move them to a second jar of clean solvent for a final rinse. That second rinse is the step people skip. Then spin each bearing by hand. Never blast a dry bearing with compressed air. That party trick has ruined more bearings than any puddle.

scenes.heading: One drop of oil is enough
scenes.narration: Step four is drying, and it decides whether your work was worth it. Solvent left inside thins the new oil, and water left inside starts rust straight away. Lay the bearings on a clean cloth and give them time. Warmth helps. Strong heat does not. Step five is oil, and here less is more. Use one drop per bearing, then spin it slowly by hand to spread it. On screen you can see why. One drop finds the raceway and rolls clean. A flooded bearing collects dust and drags. Step six. Press the seals back in evenly until they click and sit flush. Refit the wheels. If a wheel spun well on the bench but binds once bolted in, your axle is too tight or your spacers are wrong.

scenes.heading: What to clean bearings with
scenes.narration: A good bearing cleaner has two jobs. It must dissolve old oil and carry grit away, and then it must leave completely. Four options pass. A dedicated bearing cleaner is the easy answer. A citrus based degreaser is gentle on nylon cages. White spirit is strongest on thick old grease, but it needs a patient, full dry. And ninety nine percent isopropyl alcohol flashes off fast and leaves nothing, so it suits a quick refresh. Now the list to keep away. Acetone, which is in most nail polish remover, attacks nylon cages and rubber seals. Petrol, diesel and kerosene leave an oily film. Brake cleaner strips the steel bare. And water, soap and dishwashers are the worst of all.

scenes.heading: Habits for a cleaner job
bullets: Two labelled jars: wash, then rinse
Gloves and moving air
Keep solvent away from your oil
Settle and reuse clean solvent
scenes.narration: Why is acetone such a trap? Because it is a superb degreaser. A cage bathed in acetone can look perfect and then crack under load two weeks later. Water is the worst because it reaches every surface inside a bearing and then refuses to leave any of them. A few habits make the whole job cleaner. Use two sealed, labelled jars, so you never top up the rinse with dirty solvent. Wear gloves and work in moving air. Keep the solvent and the oil well apart on the bench, because oil with a splash of solvent in it is no longer the oil you bought. Let the jars stand so the grit settles, reuse the clean solvent from the top, and dispose of the sludge properly, never down a drain.

scenes.heading: Your seal decides your method
scenes.narration: Not every bearing comes apart. Look at one in good light and work out which of three types you have. A rubber seal that lifts out is the easy case, and you get the full six step clean. A metal shield needs judgement. Many have a thin retaining ring you can lift first. But if the shield resists and starts to bend, stop. A bent shield rubs on the balls forever. Bearings you cannot open get a flush instead. Agitate them longer, change to fresh solvent, agitate again, and dry them for longer than feels necessary. Then put a drop of oil at the gap by the inner race and turn it slowly. A flush never reaches what a full clean does, so do it more often.

scenes.heading: How often to clean
bullets: Dry indoor track: every couple of months
Outdoor roads: monthly
Dusty or humid: more often
After water: that same evening
scenes.narration: How often should you do this? It depends on where you skate. On a clean, dry indoor track, every couple of months is usually plenty. On outdoor roads and mixed surfaces, clean monthly, or whenever the roll changes. Anywhere dusty, gritty or humid, clean more often and check after every hard week. After any contact with water, clean them that evening, no exceptions. A quick drop of oil between full cleans is fine. And ceramic bearings need this care too. The balls are harder than steel, but the races are still steel, the cage is still nylon, and the seals still let dirt in. A dirty ceramic bearing can even damage its own races faster, so clean ceramic on the same schedule as steel.

scenes.heading: When to replace, not clean
bullets: Rust or pitting after a clean
Gritty, notchy feel when turned slowly
Play between the races
Damaged cage or a seal that will not seat
scenes.narration: Cleaning extends a bearing's life, but it does not make it last forever. Retire a bearing if you see rust or pitting that survives a proper clean. Retire it if it still feels gritty or notchy when you turn it slowly, even after cleaning and oiling. Retire it if the inner and outer race rock against each other, if the cage is damaged, or if a seal will not seat any more. A damaged cage can fail suddenly and take the bearing with it. If only one bearing in a wheel is bad, replace the pair in that wheel at least. And brand new bearings usually need no cleaning. They come with the right lubricant inside, so adding oil on top just makes a heavier mix.

scenes.heading: Quick answers
bullets: WD40 is not a lubricant
Quiet does not mean fast
Dry for hours, oil the same day
Never let an air line spin them
scenes.narration: A few quick answers. Can you use WD40 or household oil? Please do not. WD40 is a water displacer, not a lubricant, and household oils are too heavy for a speed bearing. Your bearings sound fine but feel slow? Clean them anyway. Thick old oil can drag without making noise, because noise is a late symptom. How long should they dry? Until there is no smell of solvent and no damp anywhere, which means hours. A fan helps more than heat. And oil them the same day you clean them, because a freshly cleaned bearing is bare steel that can rust overnight.

scenes.heading: Spin a wheel every week and listen
scenes.sub: Full guide at livelica.com, link in the description
scenes.narration: If you take one thing from this, make it the spin test. Every week, pick up a wheel and spin it. Listen, feel, and compare it to the others. If it sounds gritty or stops sooner than it used to, it is telling you something. That ten second habit catches bearing problems at the stage where a clean and one drop of oil fixes them completely. The full guide, with every solvent and seal type explained, is on the LiveLica blog. The link is in the description.
